body:
Ardent BJP supporters too are no fans of India's Education Minister, Mr Dharmendra Pradhan. The opposition exists in a democracy to raise issues against the ruling government, so why would they leave the chance to ask for the resignation of Mr Pradhan. In all this, the online moment of Cockroach Janta Party, sensed an oppurtunity and they went all guns blazing. Again, completely regular and obvious thing to do in a democracy. They sensed the burning issue affecting the youth of India, and had also the support of the parents of these youngsters, which was the NEET leak scandal.

BJP top brass did not budge and stuck to backing it's blue eyed Education Minister. This only worked better for CJP and it's handlers, and they took the movement offline.

As the imprints of AAP and connections with it's top leaders became more clear, the public did not give it the support which Dipke thought they would.

However since the issue of Pradhan not being sacked has hit a raw nerve among the youth, there are various groups within the protestors who now have come together. The AAPturnists, professional protestors, life is a protest Yogendra Yadav types, emotionally charged youth, the mischief makers, members from opposition, vandals and the regular youth who are fed up.

So now we have a situation, where majority agrees that the cause is a righteous one but the same majority is extremely sceptical of the players driving this protest.

What we saw today is the intersection of State-Ruling government-Peaceful protestors-Criminals-Negotiations-Opposition which in a nutshell my friend is called a Democracy.

body:
Why didn't #Vijay i.e. CM of TN support the 
#JantarMantarprotest ?

#CMVijay had already written to the #PM seeking steps to ban #NEET as soon as he became Chief Minister. So, his stand against #NEET is already clear.

Now, coming to the #CJP protest, it has three demands:
1. Release #SonamWangchuk 
2. Provide ₹1 crore compensation to the affected students' families.
3. Resignation of the Education Minister.

I agree with the first two demands. But I am skeptical about the third.

A paper leak occurred, investigations were conducted, those responsible were identified, and action was taken. The system is also being moved towards Computer-Based Tests with stronger encryption reduce such incidents.

If the demand was to #BanNEET because the system itself is flawed, we should support that. But demanding only a minister's resignation doesn't solve the root problem.

If #CMVijay supports this, it would set a dangerous precedent. Tomorrow, every issue could simply become a demand for a minister's resignation. Which is not justified !!!

Ministers can change. Unless the system is corrected, the same issue can happen again under someone else. 

I'm not a blind supporter of #CJP. I have my own reservations.

So, when I myself have doubts, I understand why #CMVijay chose not to comment.

That said, the protest should never have turned violent. The ruling Central Government i.e. #BJP must take responsibility for that.

POV : I'm not a #BJP supporter. This is simply my personal opinion.

@CMOTamilnadu @TVKVijayHQ

I fully endorse the views expressed by @annamalai_k. Protest is a democratic right, but timely dialogue and addressing people is the responsibility of a democratic government.

The question that deserves an answer is simple: Why does meaningful engagement so often come only after a crisis escalates?

As an Ex-Serviceman, I have witnessed this pattern repeatedly. Since 2015, veterans have peacefully protested at Jantar Mantar over issues such as OROP implementation and other long pending grievances. Farmers have protested. Students have protested. In each case, many participants raised genuine concerns that deserved timely engagement.

We should not dismiss every protester as "anti national" simply because some individuals and political parties may attempt to hijack a movement. The law must deal firmly with those who incite violence or attack police, journalists, or public property. But genuine grievances should never be ignored because of the actions of a few.

I am often attacked on social media for expressing these views. Let me be clear: I am a nationalist. My loyalty is to the Nation, not to any individual or political party.

Supporting the government when it is right and questioning it when it falls short are both acts of patriotism.

Despite repeated representations, this government has neither resolved the genuine grievances of ex servicemen nor fully complied with many judgments of the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT), the High Courts, and the Supreme Court. 

Leadership is measured not only by decisive action, but also by the willingness to listen. Humility strengthens leadership; "high headedness" creates distance between a government and its people. India's youth, farmers, and veterans deserve to be heard before frustration turns into unrest.

Nation First. Truth First. Always. 🇮🇳

Over the past many years, I have taken a personal stand in support of the NEET examination, arguing that it brought uniformity in student selection across the country and gave students from underprivileged backgrounds a real shot at pursuing their dream of medical education. In the last 5 years, the NEET UG question paper has leaked thrice. Imagine the amount of pressure that it puts on students, who had to go through the examination process yet another time when the system that was supposed to bring in uniformity was failing. Yet there was no accountability, and I believe strongly that it was that moment that brought in a shift in the minds of the students to take to the streets to cry their hearts out. 

Protest is a fundamental right in a Democracy. The pertinent question, however, is this: why did the BJP-led Central Government take so long to initiate a dialogue with the protestors? Why was meaningful engagement delayed until the protest had escalated to a flashpoint? What kept you waiting?

The students and the people who are leading them also have a responsibility here. It is natural that when a protest stays on for weeks, people with vested interests will take the stage to air views that are either completely irrelevant to the initial demands of the protests or would try to completely hijack it to serve their agenda. If you remain silent and let these people with vested interests further their agenda, then you are deviating from your core objectives. Please do not let it happen!

I urge the BJP-led Central Government to engage in meaningful dialogue, uphold transparency, and take swift, appropriate action to address the concerns at hand. The strength of any nation lies in the confidence its youth place in its institutions. If our students lose faith in the fairness and credibility of our education system, we are jeopardising the future of our nation.

body:
Let me give you a reality check.

India has seen protests before. But this one is different.

Earlier, many mass movements were led by people who already had stable jobs, financial security, and a safety net. They could afford to spend days on the streets because losing one week didn’t mean losing their future.

Today’s youth don’t have that privilege.

Many of the faces you saw at the CJP protest weren’t just NEET aspirants. Some were former aspirants. Some had spent 6, 8, even 10 years preparing for one competitive exam after another. Some crossed 30. Some exhausted their savings. Some watched friends move on while they remained trapped in an endless cycle of forms, postponements, paper leaks, vacancies that never came, and recruitment processes that stretched for years.

People mock them by asking, “Does a 30 year old look like a NEET aspirant?”

No. They look like the outcome of a broken system with nothing to lose. 

They look like someone who was told since childhood that education would change their life, only to discover that merit means little when exams are repeatedly cancelled, recruitment is delayed, and opportunities keep shrinking.

History shows the same pattern.

The JP Movement of the 1970s wasn’t just about politics. It was fuelled by students angry over unemployment, inflation, corruption, and a government that had stopped listening.

The Mandal Commission protests were about more than reservations, they reflected deep anxiety over limited government jobs and a generation terrified about its future.

Across the world, whether it was the Arab Spring or student-led movements in Europe and Latin America, prolonged unemployment and the feeling of having no future became powerful forces behind public unrest.

When an entire generation starts believing that hard work no longer guarantees dignity, the problem is no longer individual failure. It becomes a failure of governance.

A government cannot promise every citizen a government job.

But it is responsible for creating opportunities, conducting fair and timely recruitment, protecting the integrity of examinations, and ensuring that young people don’t spend the best years of their lives waiting for a result that never arrives.

Hope is not built through slogans.

Hope is built when effort is rewarded.

And when that hope disappears, frustration doesn’t stay inside coaching classrooms forever.

One day, it reaches the streets.

When thousands of young people decide that protesting feels more meaningful than studying for the next exam, that should alarm every government, regardless of which party is in power.

Because the biggest crisis isn’t unemployment.

It’s a generation slowly losing faith that tomorrow will be better than today 🙏🏻

Sanam Shetty has exposed what she describes as the agenda of DMK agents who sought to divert the protest for political purposes. While CJP members have been protesting in Delhi for over 20 days, many of those who had spent the same period discussing and celebrating the FIFA World Cup and new film releases suddenly chose to unleash their hostility when the subject became Vijay. Sanam Shetty has exposed the double standards of these individuals.

The students protest is gradually being diverted from its original purpose. Particularly in Tamilnadu, efforts are being made to steer it in a different direction. While the CJP protesters and the students are demanding only the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, some individuals, unable to come to terms with their political defeat, are using the movement as an outlet for their resentment. By calling this out openly, Sanam Shetty has exposed these elements, and she deserves appreciation for doing so.

body:
Nine years ago, S Anitha became the first victim of NEET in Tamil Nadu, and one of the most prominent faces of Tamil Nadu’s fight against NEET.

In 2017, the 17-year-old from Ariyalur had scored 1,176 out of 1,200 marks in her Class 12 Tamil Nadu State Board exams. Her medical cut-off score was 196.75 out of 200 — marks that would have placed her among medical aspirants under Tamil Nadu’s earlier admission system.

But that year, NEET became mandatory for medical admissions. Anitha, who had prepared through the state-board syllabus, could not secure a medical seat through the national entrance exam. She became one of the earliest voices opposing NEET in Tamil Nadu, arguing that a common entrance test would disadvantage students from rural areas, government schools and marginalised communities.

Anitha’s brother S. Manirathnam, who has now joined the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi, says her fight was deeply personal.

He says Anitha was raised by their father, a daily wage labourer, after their mother died when she was seven. He recalls that Anitha wanted to become a doctor because their mother’s death due to an illness had shaped her dream of entering medicine.

“She wanted to become a doctor because she had seen the suffering caused by the lack of medical care,” Manirathnam said, recalling his sister’s journey.

Anitha joined the legal battle against NEET and became one of the petitioners before the Supreme Court, seeking relief for Tamil Nadu students. The Court did not grant the exemption sought by the state, and days later, on 1 September 2017, Anitha died by suicide at her home in Ariyalur.

Speaking about the impact of NEET on his family, Manirathnam said, “NEET has destroyed my family.”

Years later, he has joined the CJP protest, saying Tamil Nadu’s opposition to NEET began with students like Anitha, who questioned whether a single national entrance exam could account for the inequalities faced by students across the country.

He is Vibhu Gautam.

He made abusive remarks against the Indian Army during the CJP protest.

After his video went viral, some people decided that he should be handed over to the police. However, when they went to his house, they found out that his father is disabled. Seeing his father's situation, they decided not to pursue getting him arrested. Instead, they asked him to apologize, and he later recorded and posted a video apologizing.

Is it wrong to protest against the NEET paper leak or to demand the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan? No, not at all.

But that is not what he did. Instead, he came to the protest and started making abusive remarks against the Indian Army. He is not a child who cannot distinguish between right and wrong. He is old enough to understand the remarks he is making and the legal consequences of his actions.

His mindset led him to believe that it was the moment to turn India into another Nepal or Bangladesh. Many people like him also fail to understand that when they move away from the actual cause of a protest and engage in propaganda and anti-India activities, they may face serious legal consequences. Their careers and futures could be affected. In his case, even his father had to apologize because of his son's actions.

This period of unrest is temporary. The protests will eventually end. Those with political ambitions will move on and continue with politics. But common people like us may end up facing the consequences.

In the end, all that remains is regret.
By the time you realize the cost of your actions, the damage is already done. It can leave behind years of legal trouble, a damaged reputation, lost opportunities, and a burden that lasts far longer than the protest itself.

body:
Nine years ago, S Anitha became the first victim of NEET in Tamil Nadu, and one of the most prominent faces of Tamil Nadu’s fight against NEET.

In 2017, the 17-year-old from Ariyalur had scored 1,176 out of 1,200 marks in her Class 12 Tamil Nadu State Board exams. Her medical cut-off score was 196.75 out of 200 — marks that would have placed her among medical aspirants under Tamil Nadu’s earlier admission system.

But that year, NEET became mandatory for medical admissions. Anitha, who had prepared through the state-board syllabus, could not secure a medical seat through the national entrance exam. She became one of the earliest voices opposing NEET in Tamil Nadu, arguing that a common entrance test would disadvantage students from rural areas, government schools and marginalised communities.

Anitha’s brother S. Manirathnam, who has now joined the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi, says her fight was deeply personal.

He says Anitha was raised by their father, a daily wage labourer, after their mother died when she was seven. He recalls that Anitha wanted to become a doctor because their mother’s death due to an illness had shaped her dream of entering medicine.

“She wanted to become a doctor because she had seen the suffering caused by the lack of medical care,” Manirathnam said, recalling his sister’s journey.

Anitha joined the legal battle against NEET and became one of the petitioners before the Supreme Court, seeking relief for Tamil Nadu students. The Court did not grant the exemption sought by the state, and days later, on 1 September 2017, Anitha died by suicide at her home in Ariyalur.

Speaking about the impact of NEET on his family, Manirathnam said, “NEET has destroyed my family.”

Years later, he has joined the CJP protest, saying Tamil Nadu’s opposition to NEET began with students like Anitha, who questioned whether a single national entrance exam could account for the inequalities faced by students across the country. 

@hey_eshwar reports.

2. This is the Saurabh Das who praises Umar Khalid, calls him "brave," and says that Umar Khalid spent five years in jail on baseless charges. He also describes this as a permanent blot on the Indian judiciary.

3. Now, let me tell you who Umar Khalid is.

4. Umar Khalid is currently lodged in Delhi's Tihar Jail.

Umar Khalid is often described by his critics as a leader of the so-called "Tukde-Tukde Gang," and it has been alleged that on 9 February 2016, the following slogans were raised at the JNU campus:

- Slogans against the Indian Army.
- Slogans against the CRPF.
- "Azaadi, Azaadi."
- "Afzal, your blood will bring a revolution."
- "Afzal, we are ashamed; your killers are still alive."
- "India will be broken into pieces, Inshallah, Inshallah."

Now let me tell you who Afzal Guru was.

Afzal Guru was a Kashmiri separatist who was convicted for his role in the conspiracy behind the 2001 terrorist attack on the Indian Parliament.

The major allegations and details of the case are as follows:

On 13 December 2001, five terrorists belonging to Jaish-e-Mohammed attacked the Indian Parliament. Eight security personnel and one gardener were martyred in the attack.

Afzal Guru was convicted on charges that he was an active member of Jaish-e-Mohammed and had provided weapons, shelter, and logistical support to the terrorists involved in the Parliament attack.

He was executed by hanging in Delhi's Tihar Jail on 9 February 2013.

It is also alleged that during the 9 February 2016 JNU event, Umar Khalid supported Afzal Guru through slogans such as:

- "Afzal, your blood will bring a revolution."
- "Afzal, we are ashamed; your killers are still alive."

I am sharing all of this so that you can understand the point I am trying to make.

Saurabh Das supports Umar Khalid, against whom allegations of the above-mentioned anti-India slogans have been made.

Now, I also want to tell you that, in my opinion, many of the people protesting at Jantar Mantar are associated with the same so-called "Tukde-Tukde Gang."

I only want to urge all of you to stay aware and think carefully.

Today, in the name of education-related issues and the NEET paper leak, ask yourselves whose voices are being heard at Jantar Mantar.

If this is truly only an education-related movement, then think carefully about what the following slogans have to do with students' issues:

- "Azaadi, Azaadi."
- "Only the name of Allah will remain."
- "Down with BJP."
- "Down with RSS."
- "Down with Modi."
- "Down with Amit Shah."
- "Down with Brahminism."
- "We will uproot Parliament."
- "We will turn India into Nepal and Bangladesh."

In my opinion, the protest at Jantar Mantar is increasingly becoming a platform for people whose mindset is anti-national, and a means of supporting such individuals.

I believe that, through the guise of this student movement, a deeper conspiracy is being carried out to weaken India and the temple of our democracy—the Parliament—and to push the country toward situations similar to those seen in Nepal and Bangladesh.

Therefore, I humbly request all of you to think, understand, and analyse the situation for yourselves. Do not become a part of any political strategy without careful consideration.

Otherwise, the future of every student and every young person may be affected.

I simply want to say: do not become anyone's pawn. Think for yourself, understand the facts, reflect carefully, and secure your own future.

Do not become a victim of political manipulation.

Jai Hind. Jai Bharat. ❤️🙏

Certain NEET students circulated AI-manipulated OMR sheets falsely alleging flaws in the examination process, a claim that was thoroughly debunked by the NTA with facts and data. 

Instead of being a genuine academic issue, this fabricated controversy became the perfect trigger for opportunistic Leftist and radical elements who were already lying in wait. These groups, often acting as vultures on sensitive student matters, quickly converted peaceful student concerns into violent protests in Delhi involving stone-pelting, vandalism of public property, and attempts to create law-and-order chaos. Police were forced to intervene firmly to protect citizens and restore order.

The students who spread these misleading AI-altered sheets deserve to be publicly named and shamed. Their actions did not help any aspirant; they deliberately misled the nation and provided cover for anti-social elements to create violence.

In a classic display of hypocrisy and cowardice, the CJP founders sensed trouble brewing from the unrest they had helped stoke and desperately reached out to the Modi govt at 11:50 AM. The government directed them to meet Union Minister J.P. Nadda. The CJP team comprising Das & Ranka was made to wait for two full hours in his office before being granted time, a clear indication that the government was not going to entertain their drama on priority.

While they were busy seeking government intervention, their so-called leaders were nowhere to be seen on the ground. Vijeta Dahiya was spotted elsewhere, and Dipke was hiding behind the stage. All the prominent CJP founders conveniently disappeared from the protest sites after they had instigated and radicalised the mobs to turn violent. This is their standard modus operandi: incite from the shadows, let students and hired elements do the dirty work of stone-pelting and vandalism, and vanish the moment police action begins.

This episode once again exposes CJP as professional agitators who have zero concern for actual students or merit-based examinations. They hijack genuine or manufactured grievances, inject radical elements into the protests, create violence on the streets, and then run to the very government they abuse for protection and photo-ops. Their leaders’ absence from the scene while mobs attacked police and damaged property speaks volumes about their character. 
They acted as instigators, not leaders.

Delhi Police is now systematically scanning CCTV footage to identify every stone-pelter, vandal, and troublemaker. Those who participated in violence must be booked under the strictest provisions. At the same time, the role of organisations like CJP in converting a student issue into street violence needs thorough investigation. Spreading AI-generated misinformation to trigger unrest, radicalising protests, and then abandoning the very people they misled is not activism; it is criminal irresponsibility.

A thread which you shouldn't ignore ,

Cockroach Janta Party and Role of AI :-

15th may 2026- CJI remarks about parasites and Cockroaches.

16th may 2026-   Abhijit Dipke ( Political communication graduate) launched Cockroach janta party.

He warned "What will happen if all Cockroaches unite"

The most important point ( Role of Algorithm Amplification)

-With the help of Meta and  X, Cockroach Janta Party gained massive popularity

By utilizing generative AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT to design a mock manifesto and promotional images, the CJP fed the recommendation engines high-engagement, satirical content.

Within 72 hours ,they got 3 million followers on Instagram 

And

After 5 days, , it surpassed 10 million followers, overtaking the official Instagram handle of the ruling BJP.

Later,

Within two weeks, the account had amassed over 22 million followers on Instagram.

On X (formerly Twitter), the official account garnered around 90,000 followers in under a week before facing government blocking orders on June 21, 2026.

At the exact same time, India was dealing with a devastating crisis surrounding the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) for medical students. Widespread leaks of the exam papers forced millions of students into retakes, and the crushing pressure was linked to dozens of student suicides. This disaster was compounded by a severe job crisis, with nearly 40% of Indian graduates under the age of 25 facing unemployment.

Fusing digital satire with genuine public grievance, the CJP used its vast digital infrastructure to organize real-world, offline protests across the country, channeling the collective anger over the NEET crisis.

On July20, 2026: The movement culminated in a massive "Sansad Chalo" (March to Parliament) in New Delhi. Operating under the CJP banner, the youth formalized their demands regarding the NEET crisis.

 They specifically demanded the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, the release of allied activist Sonam Wangchuk, and ₹1 crore in compensation for the families of the students who died by suicide following the leaks.

Our Legal Enforcement agencies ( LEA) 
were not at all prepared for this.

They were banking on their old modus operandi to block internet and hence contain the  spread of information. 

However, the agitators used a different mode of communication, "Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)", which could communicate with their peers using an app which does not require internet and hence maintained coordination.

The blame lies squarely with LEAs and MeitY for failing to flag the sudden surge in downloads—a failure made even more glaring given that the American embassy had already predicted the disruptions. 

MeitY has the infrastructure to do so (flag the surge of app downloads for Bluetooth communication)  where as our LEA lacks the technology to block it.

Consumer-grade Bluetooth mesh apps (like Bridgefy, FireChat, and Bitchat) were fundamentally popularized by civilian protest movements seeking to bypass government-imposed internet shutdowns.

Bridgefy saw massive spikes in downloads during India's Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) protests and during election-related internet blackouts in Uganda.

In these scenarios, Law Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) and state intelligence services have actively deployed the BDoS (Bluetooth Denial of Service), traffic analysis, and Sybil attacks discussed earlier to de-anonymize users and break the mesh routing.

body:
The CJP (Cockroach Janta Party) protest at Jantar Mantar is overwhelmingly focused on student issues: alleged paper leaks in NEET/NET/CUET/CBSE exams, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation, exam reforms, ₹1 crore compensation for families of students who died by suicide, and student mental health.

**Non-student/broader issues raised include:**
- Demand for immediate release of climate activist Sonam Wangchuk (who joined with an indefinite hunger strike) after his alleged forcible removal by authorities.
- Escalation to demand Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s resignation over handling of protests and systemic failures.
- Appeals to farmers and civil society for solidarity, noting past mutual support between student and farmer movements.
- Calls for overall government accountability, transparency in institutions, and a peaceful “Chalo Sansad” march to Parliament.

The core CJP movement also has a wider manifesto on judicial/electoral reforms, but these have not been central to the current Jantar Mantar agitation.

body:
The government was under the impression that re-conducting NEET alone would resolve students' grievances regarding the paper leak.

This is precisely why Cockroach Janta Party was ‘allowed’ to protest, and Sonam Wangchuk was ‘permitted’ to go on a hunger strike (who had done it 3 times before, albeit unsuccessfully).

In that way, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan did not need to resign, and people would eventually move on to a different issue.

After all, it wasn’t the first time that an exam was compromised and generated public outrage.

The government hoped that the movement would fizzle out on its own. Because if it gave in to one demand, it might have to agree to others.

So, the government watched in silence as the number of protestors swelled. Sonam Wangchuk’s hunger strike crossed 3 weeks.

On social media, it became one man’s fight against the mighty State. This demand for accountability grew consistently.

People could freely back CJP as it did not have political baggage (Abhijeet Dipke’s connection to AAP appeared trivial before the core issue of the paper leak).

And for the first time in many years (after the CAA and farm laws), a protest had grown in magnitude unforeseen by the government.

The public resentment quadrupled after what transpired during the march to Parliament (only if you look beyond the echo chamber on Twitter).

It was clear that the indifference and lack of acknowledgement of the protests was no longer going to work.

As a result, Union Health Minister JP Nadda met not just the CJP spokespersons but also the students who were injured during the rally.

The core issue of the protest is non-political, even though many politicians and activists have frequented Jantar Mantar so far.

This is why I am seeing a large number of fence-sitters and apolitical folks throwing their weight behind Sonam Wangchuk.

You cannot convince anyone otherwise because it is too little and too late now.

Let us not forget that farm laws had to be rolled back and CAA remained in limbo for several years due to the large-scale protests.

Unless Dharmendra Pradhan resigns, this new wave of demonstrations is unlikely to stop.

Any further use of police force against students is going to make matters worse.

By injecting politics into the protest and attempting to portray the students movement as one against the #TVKVijay‌ government, those who directed their hostility toward Chief Minister Vijay and the TVK administration have now been exposed by actress @ungalsanam.

At a time when the protest against the alleged #NEET question paper leak was meant to remain focused solely on that issue, some participants carried placards reading, 'We need JanaNayagam, not JanaNayagan,' thereby politicizing the students movement. Sanam Shetty has exposed what she describes as the agenda of DMK agents who sought to divert the protest for political purposes. While CJP members have been protesting in Delhi for over 20 days, many of those who had spent the same period discussing and celebrating the FIFA World Cup and new film releases suddenly chose to unleash their hostility when the subject became Vijay. Sanam Shetty has exposed the double standards of these individuals.

The students protest is gradually being diverted from its original purpose. Particularly in Tamilnadu, efforts are being made to steer it in a different direction. While the CJP protesters and the students are demanding only the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, some individuals, unable to come to terms with their political defeat, are using the movement as an outlet for their resentment. By calling this out openly, Sanam Shetty has exposed these elements, and she deserves appreciation for doing so.

दिल्ली पुलिस ने 20 जुलाई 2026 का CCTV फुटेज जारी किया है, जिसमें पार्लियामेंट के पास "कॉकरोच पार्टी अटैक" के दौरान की घटनाएँ दिखाई गई हैं।

फुटेज और पुलिस के बयान के अनुसार, हमलावरों को पार्लियामेंट की ओर बढ़ने की कोशिश करते समय बैरिकेड्स पर रोक दिया गया था। पुलिस की तैनाती के बावजूद, वीडियो में कुछ प्रदर्शनकारियों को कथित तौर पर बैरिकेड्स गिराते, उनके ऊपर से कूदते और आगे बढ़ते हुए दिखाया गया है। पुलिस ने कहा कि इसके कारण भीड़ को कंट्रोल करने के लिए लाठीचार्ज करना पड़ा।

अधिकारियों के बयान से साफ होता है कि टकराव तब शुरू हुआ जब प्रदर्शनकारियों ने बैरिकेड्स और पुलिस वालों पर हमला किया, न कि इसका उल्टा हुआ। 20/07/2026 12:35:00 का CCTV टाइमस्टैम्प उस पल को कैप्चर करता है जब हमला हुआ।

CJP प्रोटेस्ट, जिसे "अभिजीत दिपके" ने शुरू किया था, NEET 2026 पेपर लीक और एग्जामिनेशन सुधारों से जुड़ी मांगों को लेकर जंतर-मंतर पर चल रहा है। फुटेज जारी करने से पहले सोशल मीडिया पर उस दिन हिंसा किसने शुरू की, इस बारे में अलग-अलग बातें चल रही थीं।

दिल्ली पुलिस ने कहा कि यह कार्रवाई शांति बनाए रखने के लिए की गई थी।  कानून और व्यवस्था बनाए रखने और हाई-सिक्योरिटी ज़ोन के पास किसी भी तरह की हिंसा को रोकने के लिए।

Delhi Police has released CCTV footage from 20th July 2026 showing events during the "Cockroach  Party Attack near Parliament.

According to the footage and police statement, Attacker were stopped at barricades while attempting to move towards Parliament. Despite police deployment, the video shows some protesters allegedly bringing down the barricades, jumping over them, and moving forward. Police said this led to a lathi-charge to control the crowd.

The statement from authorities clarifies that the confrontation began after protesters attacked the barricades and police personnel, and not the other way around. The CCTV timestamp of 20/07/2026 12:35:00 captures the moment of the breach.

The CJP protest, founded by "Abhijit Dipke", has been ongoing at Jantar Mantar over demands related to the NEET 2026 paper leak and examination reforms. The release of footage comes amid conflicting narratives circulating on social media about who initiated the violence that day.

Delhi Police said the action was taken to maintain law and order and prevent a breach near a high-security zone.

22. Who is CJP to demand the Prime Minister's resignation? He was democratically elected. What is the connection between his resignation and NEET?

23. What are the "usual suspects" doing at Jantar Mantar? Farooq Abdullah is demanding statehood for Jammu (amidst the NEET protest), Kejriwal is promising the best lawyers (who will pay for this, and for whom will the lawyers appear?), Akhilesh Yadav, and—as always—the Bollywood gang of anti-nationals (I wonder if any of their children have been affected). Dimple Yadav perhaps did not show as much sympathy for her husband, Akhilesh, as she did for certain "peaceful" protesters—a great photo opportunity for all involved.

24. Why did the top three "head cockroaches" vanish when the violence erupted? Was it not a convenient time for burgers, meetings, and the like?

25. Which minority group possesses such expertise in stone-pelting that truckloads of stones were seized? If this was meant to be a peaceful protest, what were trucks filled with stones doing there? And how much time, money, and effort does all this require? It could hardly have been a spur-of-the-moment decision; careful planning would have been the preferred route.

26. Why were truckloads of stones seized from CJP supporters? What were the stones for? They weren't ordinary stones but specially shaped ones designed to be thrown like boomerangs.

27. What was being carried in the CJP supporters' backpacks? Stones, undoubtedly.

28. Why were police vehicles and equipment destroyed? Who pays for this?

29. Why did the US State Department warn its citizens two days in advance—on July 19 and 20—to avoid the Jantar Mantar area? What did they know that we didn't? After all, the perpetrator always knows what is coming next.

body:
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Friday hardened its stand in talks with the Centre, declaring that Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation remains a non-negotiable demand and warning that protests over the NEET paper leak would intensify if its demands are not met.

CJP spokespersons Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka held a two-hour meeting with Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh at Vithalbhai Patel House, the third round of discussions this week aimed at resolving the ongoing agitation.

The meeting came hours after the Union Cabinet cleared a draft bill proposing stricter punishment for paper leaks, following Prime Minister Narendra Modi's midnight video message announcing that the legislation would be introduced in Parliament.

Despite the move, Das said the "strictest action" would be Pradhan's removal. He said protests at Jantar Mantar would continue until the minister resigned.

In a letter submitted to the government, the CJP reiterated three "non-negotiable" demands: Pradhan's resignation, Rs 1 crore compensation for NEET victims and assurance of no legal action against protesters. It also sought public apologies from the government, the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi Police Commissioner over the alleged use of force against students during the July 20 protest.

Nadda said the ministers had heard the demands and would respond after further consultations. Another meeting is scheduled for Saturday.

The CJP also urged the Centre to consider its five-point charter on examination reforms, saying structural changes were essential to restore public confidence in the education system.

With protests continuing at Jantar Mantar, security has been tightened in the national capital. Additional CRPF companies have been airlifted to Delhi, while the CISF has curtailed leave for personnel deployed in the Delhi Metro. Internet and metro services were disrupted in several areas during the day.

The CJP also announced plans to launch a website to collect evidence of the July 20 police action and pursue legal proceedings against personnel accused of excesses. Meanwhile, the RAF said it had initiated an inquiry into allegations of disproportionate force during the crackdown.

May 15, 2026 — the Chief Justice of India said unemployed youth are 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀. That word became a movement.

Today — the same court, same CJI. A lawyer walks in with a video of those same students being lathi-charged on their way to Parliament.

The response, on record:

→ "𝗪𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗻𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝘄𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗼."
→ "𝗗𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲."

There was time to name them. No time to see them.

Now hold that in one hand. In the other, hold what the CJP protest is actually about:

→ NEET 2026 — a coaching operator arrested. 𝟭𝟯𝟲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 on his phone. 𝟭𝟭𝟭 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿.
→ Rate card: 𝟱 𝗹𝗮𝗸𝗵 𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿.
→ UP Constable 2024 leak — 𝟲𝟬 𝗹𝗮𝗸𝗵 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 wrote a cancelled exam.
→ A boy studying on a borrowed phone in Kota loses to a boy whose father wired ₹5 lakh.

That's the scandal. Real. Not manufactured. Not imported.

And what's happening on top of it? Rahul Gandhi flies in for a photo. Kejriwal shows up. Diljit tweets. AAP, SP, Chandrashekhar, JNU — every anti-BJP flag gets planted in Jantar Mantar.

Because the paper leak is 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹, the political circus riding it is 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗲.

Two things can be true at once.

→ The kids have a genuine grievance India owes them.
→ The Congress ecosystem is doing what it always does — turning a school-desk crisis into a regime-change spectacle.

And in the middle of it, a court that had the time to invent an insult but not the time to look at the bruise it caused.

body:
Indian politics has once again demonstrated a law that Isaac Newton somehow overlooked: for every protest, there is an equal and opposite counter-protest. Following Rahul Gandhi's sit-in near Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence demanding Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the NEET-UG paper leak, the BJP has announced nationwide demonstrations outside Congress offices. 

According to the BJP, Rahul Gandhi violated security protocols and turned a student issue into political theatre. Their remedy? More theatre, naturally. In what could be called the Great Indian Protest Exchange Programme, one party protests outside the Prime Minister's residence, the other protests outside the opposition's offices, and television crews rejoice at another week of ready-made prime-time content. 

Somewhere along the way, the students whose grievances sparked the entire controversy seem to have been politely escorted off centre stage while politicians compete in the national championship of competitive outrage. The BJP accuses the Congress of politicising the issue; the Congress accuses the BJP of diverting attention from it. 

Meanwhile, barricades are rolled out, slogans are rehearsed, and protest banners receive more exercise than policy papers. If this trend continues, India may soon need a Ministry of Counter-Protests to regulate protests against protests against protests.

body:
T 26-155 Delhi is filled with protests, strategy vs counter strategies, where is all this heading?

Everyone was waiting for JP Nadda's press conference at 8.30pm today. The Press conference came and gone and govt did not blink. Sonam Wangchuk is left high and dry now. After 25 days of fruitless fasting, Sonam Wangchuk was looking desperately for a honorable exit and end his fast. But govt is hell bent on ensuring that Sonam is not going to easily have his way. Today around 7pm Sonam made his last desperate video message where he said that he is ready to end the fast in next couple of hours, tonight itself, if govt gives him an assurance that none of the protestors would have cases lodged against them in the protest and violence that has been happening for last 2 days. But sadly, no such explicit assurance came. Now what will Sonam do? He has no option but to continue his fast. 

What is the Cockroach Janata Party and how this movement took shape? 
To simply put, CJP is a instagram page that was created from US. The owner is one named Abhijeet Dipke who was an NRI at that time. The page picked up traction in no time and had more than 20 million followers. This has kindled hopes in the left ecosystem that if CJP goes on ground and even if 10% followers turn up then we will have 2 million people on the streets. Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh would be repeated in India. Abhijeet flew down to India. He got an agenda also. NEET paper leak. This is a Gen Z issue which will instantly catch the attention. Million of dollars were poured in and Abhijeet had a clear cut agenda - To instigate the youth and bring them onto the roads. Jantar Mantar was the venue. Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister was the target. 

Forget 2 million, not even 2000 protestors turned up which left Abhijeet scramble for help 
The action began with Abhijeet Dipke landing on 6th June in Delhi and going straight to Jantar Mantar. It was expected that lakhs will join the protest but not even 2000 came. Dipke anticipated that he would be arrested from airport itself but nothing of that sort happened. Days passed but nothing happened. Numbers were falling and went to as low as 200. Pressure was on Dipke to deliver and he scrambled for help. He needed support. That is when Sonam Wangchuk, a scientist and an educationist joined the protest and gave a lease of life to Dipke.  

Sonam started his fast onto death demanding Pradhan's resignation on 28th June and that gave a new lease of life to the protest. Sonam is not new to protests. He was always a left supporter and was involved in various protests in Kashmir and Ladakh. But this is in heart of the nation, Delhi. But crowd did not come. Sonam was fasting but food was being served 3-4 times a day at Jantar Mantar. When there was no food, hardly 100 protestors were there. But at food time, the numbers crossed 500 and went even to 1000. It was obvious. People were coming only for free food, served 3 times a day. 

Sonam was frustrated as the protest was not picking up, and Congress was keeping a distance 
There were many visitors to Jantar Mantar but most of the celebs stayed away. Efforts were made to bring film stars but they all refused. What we had were youtubers and some wanna be insta influencers, hungry for visibility. AAP was reluctant to openly support it as that could move many opposition parties away. Congress knew this game played by AAP and it was keeping a safe distance. Some of the allies of congress also like SP, Sena UBT etc also maintained a distance making sonam extremely angry. He said opposition should unite giving up their differences. But Congress was not interested. 

BJP meanwhile was allowing this, as it would serve as a pressure cooker, which will take out the pent up anger against it. Yes, paper leaks are a reality and govt failed and people are angry. If this anger is taken out in a smaller protest, which will not hit it politically, its a welcome move. Once people protest their anger also will go. That is why govt was allowing it. This situation was slowly working in govt's favor and both sonam and Abhijeet were thoroughly frustrated. They needed an exit route and that came in the form of the Parliament monsoon session. 

A peaceful protest on 20th July, when Parliament opens is the only strategy left or CJP 
Everyone was getting ready for it. Govt felt that this is the perfect end to the movement. Allow the march without Sonam and let it die a natural death. That's why Sonam was picked up 2 days before on 18th July and moved to hospital. The Delhi HC judgement asking govt to monitor his health condition was used as a pretext. This made the protest headless. That is when AAP and other left parties took over the movement. That made a apolitical movement political. What happened on 20th July was violence and stone pelting. The agitation went out of control. The crowd was there in thousands but nobody knows who they were. Nobody is sure how many of them were genuine students and how many political activists. Media reported it in full and it caught the imagination of the public. 

Congress woke up and had its parallel protest and its opposition vs opposition for next 2 days 
Just on the day of Parliament march, opposition realized how this CJP protests started to gather attention. Rahul Gandhi who was away for sometime, is back in the country and suddenly realized that there is a full meal of agitation cooked and ready in the plate. So, he jumped into it and so does Priyanka. Suddenly when AAP saw that congress was hijacking its own movement, it started criticizing congress. Congress was least bothered. It sat on a dharna and govt arrested Rahul and Priyanka. All media was flooded with this news. Sonam was sulking in the hospital, Abhijeet was suffering from vomiting's and AAP saw that if doesnt take control, then congress will totally hijack it. 

Then Rahul does the unthinkable. Yesterday evening he shifts his protest to 7, Lok Kalyan marg, the residence of PM. This is a dangerous escalation. What if unruly crowd manages to enter PM's residence? Govt responded and immediately it was suppressed. Having failed, Congress came to Parliament in black and staged a protest. Opposition parties also joined. But this is where Rahul's over-enthusiasm to grab limelight cost it. Akhilesh was angry that SP was not given any chance and he lashed out at Congress in the Parliament. Later SP joined AAP and both went to meet Sonam at the hospital and wanted to end this. The movement is going nowhere and Congress suddenly became active. Rahul is holding all press conferences alone and hogging the media limelight. 

Sonam was also desperate to end this. He sees no purpose in taking this ahead. NEET happened again, nearly 60% of the 20 lakh who appeared, cleared the exam and the admission process is also on. No point in holding onto it. Thus an exit plan was prepared. Akhilesh and Sanjay Singh of AAP prepared a letter urging Sonam to end his fast. Sonam put out a video urging the govt to not to put cases on students as a condition to end the fast. He was no longer wanting Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. Rahul Gandhi is now latched on to it and demanding it. BJP didnt blink. Nadda gave no such assurance. Now its on Sonam to decide what he will do. 

BJP has created a rift in the opposition, but this could backfire on it also 
Lot of accidents happen while handling such situations and BJP should be careful. Reference point is Anna agitation of 2012 and how it turned people against congress then. BJP can find itself in similar situation if it doesnt handle it well. Yes, opposition is divided today but who knows what happens tomorrow. Parliament is in session and BJP has a task of getting delimitation bill passed. Congress would use this agitation to derail it. Next 10 days are critical for BJP. One wrong move and all the good work done for this long will be gone. Do not take opposition lightly. Rahul wants his limelight and with UP and Punjab elections coming up, SP and AAP also want their share of limelight. Will all this bring them together or create more rift, time will only tell. But for now, unrest is spreading in Delhi and that is not good news.

body:
The day @Cockroachisback and @Wangchuk66 started the protest against the NTA and Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, (#NEETStudentProtest #NEET) it appeared to be a genuine movement focused on seeking accountability. However, over the past two days, with growing media attention, I have noticed several unrelated slogans being raised, which seem to be diverting the protest from its original purpose. Following the public war of words between @AamAadmiParty and @INCIndia, it has become evident that AAP was attempting to derive political mileage from the protest, while Congress' intervention appears to have prevented it from doing so.

A similar pattern can be seen in Tamilnadu. CJP's protest remained peaceful until some students' union joined in, claiming to support the movement. Instead of strengthening the original demand, they began reviving their long standing political campaigns rather than focusing on the issue at hand. This gives the impression that while CJP is genuinely trying to bring about change, others are attempting to use the movement for their own political interests. Slogans demanding the release of Umar Khalid, the restoration of Article 370, and the scrapping of the new FCRA law have now begun to dominate sections of the protest, while the original demands, seeking answers over the alleged question paper leak and calling for the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, appear to have taken a back seat. Sorry to say this, but this protest appears to have lost its direction. Instead of remaining focused on its original objective, it now seems to be heading towards an unknown destination. @abhijeet_dipke @GitanjaliAngmo

The movement in Delhi over the irregularities in the NEET examination has intensified after weeks of sustained protests. Left student organisations extended their solidarity and participated in the agitation from the outset, joining the movement launched by CJP activists and education activist Sonam Wangchuk. Various opposition parties and Members of Parliament subsequently joined the protest.

The CPI(M) General Secretary, together with the party's central leaders and MPs, formed a protective cordon between the police and the protesters to resist police excesses. Reports have also emerged of hired goons wielding lathis attacking protesters alongside the police.

Yesterday, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Shri Rahul Gandhi, and the Congress leadership extended their support to the protesters. The Opposition has also been trying to raise the issue of the NEET examination irregularities and the demand for the resignation of the Union Education Minister in the Lok Sabha.

The more the Union Government attempts to suppress the movement, the greater the public support it continues to receive.

Strongly condemns the arrest of the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Shri Rahul Gandhi.

body:
Disclaimer - this is going to be a highly anecdotal post. I have no macro data to support what I am going to say:

This time, vibe shift feels real.

At least in my corner of the world ie my age + socioeconomic cohort.

Many acquaintances, batchmates, and friends who've voted bjp in the past are now ruthlessly against it. Anti-incumbency, at least in my cohort, seems to be setting in.

And this includes people who are patriots, infra geeks, security hawks, and free-market advocates – all categories where bjp has objectively been better than congress.

Momentarily, recent events have overtaken all other factors and irritated a large chunk of people at least in my extended circle.

I've never seen so many mutuals attend a protest before. All of them have real jobs but took out time anyway.

I dislike CJP and its leadership. No ifs and buts on that. But on NEET (and let's detach the exam from CJP for this post) - Govt has screwed up big time. Not making an example out of Pradhan + Senior NTA officials (by suspension or whatever tools available) is an even bigger blunder.

We have witnessed turmoil in our neighborhood over the past five years. Allegedly propped up by the US, we've seen Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal undergo  "revolutions" that ended up with unelected new governments.

These regime changes did not turn out well for any of these countries, and I don't want India to join this list of instable polities.

But, with NEET (an exam that 22 lakh students gave), Govt has unintentionally created a massive social faultline and handed it on a platter to anyone willing to exploit it for social unrest. Combine this with a black box Insta algo, the US (allegedly) trying to "contain" India, and local political parties wanting to exploit any unrest possible to gain political points, and you get a perfect storm.

India will undergo a unique set of challenges during her journey from 2.5K to 10K per capita income society, domestic anti-incumbency among first/second time voters is one of them.

Again, vibe shift seems real. Highly anecdotal, but almost everyone I know is upset with the govt (on paper leaks, rightfully so), and this includes several folks who have voted bjp in the past.

Ps - I have sympathy for students who suffered from exam leaks and I want real action to be taken against the minister and govt officials responsible. No doubts. But student sentiments are also being exploited by forces for their own political gains, in which students are turning into a useful pawn.

सोनम वांगचुक से नड्डा की मुलाकात हुई. जिसके बाद वांगचुक ने जेपी नड्डा को पत्र लिखकर अपनी भूख हड़ताल समाप्त करने के लिए कुछ शर्तें रखी हैं. 

वांगचुक ने मांग की है कि दिल्ली पुलिस या सरकार की ओर से किसी भी छात्र के खिलाफ कोई कार्रवाई नहीं की जाएगी. 

जितने भी बच्चों ने NEET Paper Leak के दबाव में अपनी जान दी है, उनके परिवारों को उचित मुआवजा दिया जाए.

body:
I fully endorse the views expressed by @annamalai_k. Protest is a democratic right, but timely dialogue and addressing people is the responsibility of a democratic government.

The question that deserves an answer is simple: Why does meaningful engagement so often come only after a crisis escalates?

As an Ex-Serviceman, I have witnessed this pattern repeatedly. Since 2015, veterans have peacefully protested at Jantar Mantar over issues such as OROP implementation and other long pending grievances. Farmers have protested. Students have protested. In each case, many participants raised genuine concerns that deserved timely engagement.

We should not dismiss every protester as "anti national" simply because some individuals and political parties may attempt to hijack a movement. The law must deal firmly with those who incite violence or attack police, journalists, or public property. But genuine grievances should never be ignored because of the actions of a few.

I am often attacked on social media for expressing these views. Let me be clear: I am a nationalist. My loyalty is to the Nation, not to any individual or political party.

Supporting the government when it is right and questioning it when it falls short are both acts of patriotism.

Despite repeated representations, this government has neither resolved the genuine grievances of ex servicemen nor fully complied with many judgments of the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT), the High Courts, and the Supreme Court. 

Leadership is measured not only by decisive action, but also by the willingness to listen. Humility strengthens leadership; "high headedness" creates distance between a government and its people. India's youth, farmers, and veterans deserve to be heard before frustration turns into unrest.

Nation First. Truth First. Always. 🇮🇳

quote_body:
Over the past many years, I have taken a personal stand in support of the NEET examination, arguing that it brought uniformity in student selection across the country and gave students from underprivileged backgrounds a real shot at pursuing their dream of medical education. In the last 5 years, the NEET UG question paper has leaked thrice. Imagine the amount of pressure that it puts on students, who had to go through the examination process yet another time when the system that was supposed to bring in uniformity was failing. Yet there was no accountability, and I believe strongly that it was that moment that brought in a shift in the minds of the students to take to the streets to cry their hearts out. 

Protest is a fundamental right in a Democracy. The pertinent question, however, is this: why did the BJP-led Central Government take so long to initiate a dialogue with the protestors? Why was meaningful engagement delayed until the protest had escalated to a flashpoint? What kept you waiting?

The students and the people who are leading them also have a responsibility here. It is natural that when a protest stays on for weeks, people with vested interests will take the stage to air views that are either completely irrelevant to the initial demands of the protests or would try to completely hijack it to serve their agenda. If you remain silent and let these people with vested interests further their agenda, then you are deviating from your core objectives. Please do not let it happen!

I urge the BJP-led Central Government to engage in meaningful dialogue, uphold transparency, and take swift, appropriate action to address the concerns at hand. The strength of any nation lies in the confidence its youth place in its institutions. If our students lose faith in the fairness and credibility of our education system, we are jeopardising the future of our nation.

body: #WATCH | Delhi: On being allegedly assaulted during the CJP Parliament March on 20th July, YouTube journalist Asha Sharma claims, "…As soon as we entered, we encountered certain unruly elements. Specifically, there were very few students; it was evident that many outsiders had come solely to create a ruckus. They immediately started shouting ‘Godi Media, Godi Media’ at us... We had observed from the start that the atmosphere had been hijacked by a different agenda; the issue didn't really seem to be about NEET anymore… A young man named Aditya Anand came to us wanting to speak. He explained that he had been involved in the protest but had objected when he was pressured to use abusive language—specifically against PM Modi, Amit Shah, and Dharmendra Pradhan. He was asked to use filthy language and insults directed at PM Modi’s late mother and the wife of HM Amit Shah. Because of this objection, other protesters assaulted him… When Aditya was speaking to us, at that moment our camera shook, which is clearly visible in the video, and a young man, wearing a red T-shirt, groped me. I objected immediately, and the crowd surrounded us from all sides and surged towards me aggressively… Their main motive seemed to make us feel hopeless and break our resolve… We somehow managed to reach our vehicle and got inside, but they surrounded the car and started banging on it violently. The front windshield cracked, the side mirror was smashed, and the car sustained dents all over. They started hurling filthy abuses and shouting things…"

body:
Those who are against the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan claim that if the govt agrees to one demand, then it might have to agree to others.

History tells otherwise! The govt rolled back farm laws after months of protest. Since then, has the govt given in to any new demand of farmers?

The answer is no.  Not every protest gets popular support. And when it does,  the govt needs to agree to one or two demands or risk alienating a large section of 
the society.

After the success of Anna Hazare's hunger strike, everyone thought it could force Parliamentary legislation (Jan Lokpal Bill in that case) by way of protests.

Since then, countless activists and politicians have sat on a hunger strike with the hope that they would be the next Anna Hazare. All of them failed to get popular support.

The fear that protests or hunger strikes will force the government into submission or hold the State to ransom is not true in 99% of cases. 

But when a movement receives public support, there is no scope for the government to look the other way. Negotiations/ talks need to happen (as we witnessed during meetings between CJP spokespersons and Union Health Minister JP Nadda).

All of this Instagram ragebait,  brazen anti-incumbency and calls for overthrow of the government can be stopped right now by conceding to one or two of the demands.

Once that happens, the movement will die its own death as students and their parents get engaged in NEET counselling. The longer the matter is prolonged, the worse it will get in terms of optics. 

The time to act is NOW

body:
I taught JEE aspirants for years, so this one is very personal for me.

A paper leak is not a small crime. It robs the kid who studied for two years and hands the seat to someone who bought a PDF the night before. 

When that kid then stands on a road asking for a fair exam, brushing him off feels wrong at a gut level.

But first let me separate the two things that got tangled here, because the timeline is mixing them up.

First, what actually happened in court.

On July 22, a lawyer stood up before a Supreme Court bench headed by CJI Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana. He asked for an urgent hearing of a petition about police action against students during a march in Delhi on July 20. He said he had videos of police brutality and wanted it listed the next day.

The CJI declined. He said "Don't waste our time, and don't waste your time." When the lawyer pressed on the videos, the CJI said "We are not interested in videos, we don't have time to watch."

This was not the court hearing the case and rejecting the students. 

It was a request to jump the queue, called a mention for urgent listing. Courts turn these down constantly. They usually say file it properly and it will come up in the normal order. 

A day earlier, the Delhi High Court did the same thing with a similar plea, telling the lawyer "Don't drag the court into all this. It will come up tomorrow."

So on procedure, refusing to fast-track is routine and defensible.

But that line "not interested in videos" really stings. 

Yes, you can defend the refusal to rush and still feel that particular sentence could have been said better.

There is an irony sitting under all of this.

The group marching calls itself CJP, the Cockroach Janata Party. That name comes from the CJI himself. 

On May 15 he made a remark about unemployed youngsters being "like cockroaches" who become media, social media, RTI activists, and start attacking everyone. The protesters took that insult and wore it as a badge. 

So the very people he described are now on the street, and the case about them landed back in his court.

Now I dived deep into how how serious countries treat exam leaks.

China went the hardest.

In 2015 it changed its criminal law to make cheating on national exams a crime. Organising a leak or mass cheating can get you up to seven years in prison. 

On exam day they send police to guard the papers, jam phone signals, and run facial recognition at the gate to stop fake candidates. People actually go to jail. 

This year they arrested a man in Jiangxi just for posting fake videos claiming he had the paper.

Zimbabwe, a much poorer country, still acts hard. 

Its exam board cancels the results of anyone found with a paper beforehand and bans them for four exam sittings. 

In one recent year, eleven papers leaked and more than a hundred people were convicted, including headmasters, teachers, and even police officers. Cheats can face up to nine years.

Basically, they treat a leak as a crime against every honest student, they punish the adults in the chain who printed and sold the paper, and they make the system pay a price.

Now compare that to how our own top court handled the big one.

In 2024, NEET-UG had a confirmed leak. The Supreme Court under the previous CJI, DY Chandrachud, did not brush it off. It heard more than forty petitions. It said openly there was "no question that paper has been leaked." 

It said if the sanctity of the exam was lost, a retest would have to be ordered.

But it also refused to cancel the whole exam. The reasoning was that the CBI had found the leak limited to Patna and Hazaribagh, with about 155 confirmed beneficiaries, not a countrywide breach. 

The court said cancelling for 24 lakh students over a local leak would punish lakhs of honest kids and wreck the medical admission calendar.

You can disagree with that outcome. Many students did, and a review petition was filed. 

But the court atleast watched the evidence. It engaged with it. It made the government and the NTA answer for the number of wrongdoers and the action taken.

This week, on the protest question, a different bench said it would not even look at the videos at the listing stage.

The courtroom soundbite will get the clicks. It always does. But the thing that put teenagers on a Delhi road in July is not a bad quote. 

It is an exam system where a leak can happen, get confirmed, and still leave honest aspirants feeling like nothing changed for them.

Other countries have fixed this. 

They've made leaking the paper the crime, jailed the middlemen, and hardened the process. India still just has strong words. 

What we do not yet have is the sense, from a student's chair, that the system will protect the kid who did everything right.

Fix that, and the marches stop.

Supreme Court Declines Urgent Hearing on Plea Over Police Action During CJP Protest

The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to urgently list a petition challenging the alleged police action against students during the CJP's "Sansad Chalo" protest in Delhi.

While mentioning the matter, the petitioner's counsel sought an early hearing, arguing that videos showed alleged police excesses against protesters. Responding to the submission, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant remarked, "We are not interested in videos. We don't have time to watch videos." The bench also told the lawyer, "Don't waste our time, and don't waste your time," before declining an urgent listing.

The plea arose after clashes between protesters and police during the march to Parliament, where demonstrators were demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the alleged NEET examination paper leak. The protest saw baton charges, tear gas, and multiple injuries, leading petitioners to seek immediate intervention from the apex court.

The Supreme Court's refusal to grant an urgent hearing has triggered widespread political and public debate, with the CJI's remarks becoming the focus of national discussion.

​📢 MASS MOBILIZATION: Disillusioned youth flock to the movement in the millions. Meanwhile, the systemic crisis deepens as widespread paper leaks in the national NEET exams throw the futures of millions of students into chaos.
​❷ POLITICAL ESCALATION
​🏛️ CONGRESS STEPS IN: The Indian National Congress takes the exam leaks to the national stage. Protests led by the Youth Congress and NSUI are met with heavy-handed resistance, including water cannons in Rajasthan.
​🗣️ MASS OUTREACH: Rahul Gandhi launches a nationwide contact campaign targeting students, calling out structural failures in the education ministry to massive public turnout.
​🤝 STATE PRESSURE & BACKCHANNEL ENGAGEMENT: From abroad, Dipke posts videos alleging harassment of his family in Maharashtra and voicing fears of arrest. Soon after, behind-the-scenes channels open: state representatives and figures in Ladakh—including the Lieutenant Governor—engage with activist Sonam Wangchuk, bringing him into direct contact and alignment with Dipke.
​❸ THE CONVERGENCE AT JANTAR MANTAR
​🛬 RETURN AND PROTEST: Returning to India with swift official clearance, Dipke launches a formal protest in Delhi.
​🪧 THE CORE DEMAND: Joined by Sonam Wangchuk—who begins an indefinite hunger strike—the CJP demands the immediate resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
​👥 STUDENTS MASS ON GROUND: As Rahul Gandhi addresses packed student rallies across key hubs like Kota and Dehradun, thousands of students converge at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar over a 20-day standoff.
​❹ MISCALCULATION AND THE MARCH TO PARLIAMENT
​🏥 FORCED INTERVENTION: Police move on Sonam Wangchuk, forcibly removing him to a hospital for force-feeding as his health deteriorates.
​⚠️ UNDERESTIMATING GEN-Z: Authorities severely misjudge the influx of angry students rallying for the planned march to Parliament.
​🚨 THE CRACKDOWN: As momentum spikes, Wangchuk pivots to advocate for a Parliamentary debate rather than insisting strictly on minister resignations. Simultaneously, Dipke enters talks with BJP leadership, including party president J.P. Nadda.
​📸 VIOLENCE OUT IN THE OPEN: Outside, law enforcement cracks down heavily on the marching students. Images and videos of Gen-Z protesters being beaten go viral on social media.
​❺ DE-ESCALATION OFFERS VS. HIGH-STAKES FRICTION
​💼 THE GOVERNMENT’S OFFER: Establishments make it clear that while ministerial resignations are off the table, the government will coordinate with states to offer financial compensation to families of students who died by suicide during the exam leak crisis.
​✊ RESILIENCE ON THE GROUND: Refusing to back down, bloodied and beaten students repeatedly regroup and return to the protest lines.
​🚧 DIRECT ESCALATION: Rahul Gandhi and Congress leaders take the fight directly to the Prime Minister's residence at 7 Lok Kalyan Marg. In high-visibility chaos, Gandhi is dragged, his clothes torn and face bloodied, before being detained alongside fellow MPs.
​⚖️ THE DISCONNECT: As Opposition leaders face detainment and students endure police batons on the streets, CJP organizers operate freely, moving in and out of talks with government representatives—leaving the ultimate trajectory of the movement in sharp debate.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to urgently hear a petition seeking action over the Delhi Police crackdown on student protesters during the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) “Chalo Sansad” march, with Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant telling the petitioner not to “waste” the court’s time.

The matter was mentioned before a bench comprising CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, seeking urgent listing and suo motu intervention over the police action during Monday’s protest in the national capital.

When the lawyer argued that the case involved important issues such as the conduct of the NEET examination, alleged paper leaks and reforms in the National Testing Agency (NTA), the CJI cut him short.

“Don’t waste our time, and don’t waste your time,” the Chief Justice told the lawyer.

As the counsel referred to videos allegedly showing police assaulting student protesters and offered to submit them before the court, the bench declined to consider them.

“Don’t waste our time.”

That’s what the Supreme Court told lawyers seeking an urgent hearing on allegations of police excesses during the Delhi protest.

When asked to watch videos from the protest site, the response was: “We are not interested in videos. We don’t have time to watch.”

If allegations of police brutality during a public protest don’t deserve urgency, then what exactly does?

Courts rightly face enormous workloads, but justice delayed in matters involving fundamental rights often feels like justice denied. When citizens claim that the state has used excessive force, shouldn’t those claims at least be heard with seriousness before the moment passes?

If the judiciary won’t urgently examine allegations of abuse of power, who is supposed to hold the state accountable in real time?

This is a black-and-white issue, yet we’re unnecessarily complicating it by shifting the focus elsewhere.

You can criticize CJP or any other organization if you want. If they’ve done something wrong, hold them accountable. But that does not make the biggest issue disappear: the repeated exam paper leaks that have destroyed the futures of countless students.

Since Dharmendra Pradhan became Education Minister, multiple major exam paper leaks have occurred, yet where is the accountability? Instead of answering that question, the conversation is being diverted toward who is protesting rather than why they’re protesting.

The protest continued for nearly 30 days. Where were the bjp political leaders? How many came, met the students or publicly addressed their demands?

And no, you don’t have to be a NEET aspirant to speak against paper leaks. By that logic, only a rape victim should be allowed to speak against rape. Injustice is everyone’s concern.

Using force against students demanding accountability will never be justified. Those who support violence against peaceful protesters instead of demanding answers from those responsible are also helping normalize that injustice.

This is bigger than politics. Bigger than CJP. Bigger than any one organization.

The real issue is simple: Paper leaks. Accountability. Justice for students.
